correctness.rationale: For each number of delegations K=0,1,at least2, weighted-majority success is respectively P0,P1,q. The binomial average exactly equals q+A(1-d)^4+4Bd(1-d)^3. Its derivative 4(1-d)^2[(B-A)-(4B-A)d] has an affine nontrivial factor; B-A and B each factor into a strictly positive multiple of q-Q2 and Q3-q, respectively. Endpoint signs prove the complete strict three-regime optimum and boundaries for all p in (1/2,1), q in (p,1). One and three voters cannot have a strict interior optimum. Executable exact enumeration checks 225 cases; symbolic factorization verifies algebra, but the universal proof relies on analytic sign reasoning.

originality.rationale: The full closest 2022 five-voter single-expert primary text already proves beneficial sparse delegation with heterogeneous private competences; this known qualitative fact is not claimed new. No inspected primary source states the exact homogeneous four-voter, one-expert common-rate argmax as a piecewise function with two posterior-odds thresholds and minimal odd electorate. Equivalence, broader statements, numeric tables, and implication comparisons were conducted against that closest source and published semantic results. Residual risk remains for an equivalent independently derived special case or unpublished treatment.
residual_risks: The qualitative improvement from partial delegation, including in five-voter one-expert experiments, is known; the new statement must not be interpreted as introducing that phenomenon.
Unindexed equivalent parameter calibration or a direct algebraic corollary in wider expert-weight theory might predate this exact result.
The probabilistic policy is optimized only among independent anonymous common rates; broad optimizing mechanisms may dominate it.

value.rationale: The smallest odd expert-star electorate capable of an independently randomized strict partial-delegation optimum has five voters, and the full two-parameter calibration splits at exactly the posterior odds thresholds for two versus three ordinary signals. The explicit regime boundaries identify when independent signal diversity, mixed information pooling, or expert dictatorship is optimal under a natural locally independent delegation design. Unlike a merely illustrative finite example, it classifies a continuous open two-parameter model and a sharp minimality cutoff. Existing literature motivates sparse delegation but leaves this homogeneous competence phase calculation unstated.
